newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. assessing conditions for Iraq's oil deal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. assessing conditions for Iraq's oil deal.

text.p: U.N relief officials are in northern Iraq to see if conditions are suitable for implementing Baghdad's long-delayed oil-for-food agreement, U.N. sources said on Sunday.
They said a team led by Iraq's U.N. coordinator Gualtiero Fulcheri would return to Baghdad on Monday and send a report on Tuesday to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

The plan has been on hold because of fighting in northern Iraq in which Iraq's military backed a Kurdish faction against rivals. It ended with the Kurdistan Democratic Party emerging in charge of Iraqi Kurdistan.
"Fulcheri will see whether it is now workable for the oil plan to go ahead in northern Iraq...whether conditions there will be acceptable to our activities," one source said.

The oil-for-food plan signed last May permits Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months, with the proceeds going to pay for Gulf War reparations, other U.N. costs and Iraq's urgent humanitarian needs.
Of the $1.13 billion directed at Iraqi humanitarian needs, about $260 million were to go on Kurds in northern Iraq.

U.N. guards and officials arriving from northern Iraq said the area was now under firm KDP control. They said there were fewer checkpoints on main roads in the area, easing the flow of trucks and people within the region.

Until recently Iraqi Kurdistan was under twin embargoes - the U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Iraq in August 1990 after Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait and an internal blockade that Baghdad removed early this month.
A U.N. report issued recently said the fighting in northern Iraq had aggravated an "already dismal humanitarian situation" in Iraqi Kurdistan.
The report spoke of schools, hospitals, water and sanitation systems and government buildings being looted in Arbil and Sulaimaniya, the two main Kurdish cities in northern Iraq.
UNICEF in Baghdad said acute power shortages in Arbil after the latest fighting had rendered hospital blood banks, vaccines and medicines unusable.

"We are for a quick implementation of the plan. We can still operate in the north and our work there is going on without obstacles...and I think that is what Fulcheri will write to Boutros-Ghali," an aid source said.
The delay in implementing the oil-for-food plan has led the United Nations to seek $39.9 million in emergency aid to help civilians suffering from malnutrition and disease.
